children: fell 2.2% in the first week after the country's formal inclusion in FTSE Russell's secondary emerging market index, according to LSEG data.
The decline more than offset last week's 1% gain, with foreign investors selling more shares than they had bought in anticipation of the September 21 reclassification.

Foreign investors, who had been widely expected to increase their exposure after the upgrade, instead sold a net 2.8 trillion dong ($107.78 million) worth of shares on the Ho Chi Minh Stock Exchange, bourse data showed, after purchasing a net 2.7 trillion dong in the previous week.
The index's decline wiped about $7.4 billion off its market value up until September 24 this week, HoSE data showed.
Since the start of the year, foreign investors have cut their exposure to Vietnamese stocks by nearly $37 billion.

"The upgrade is only one factor. It does not mean capital will immediately flow into Vietnam," said Hoang Huy, equity strategist at Maybank Securities Vietnam. "Right now, interest rates remain the most important factor for the equity market," Huy added.
The transition will take place over four stages through 2027, with 10% of Vietnam's weighting added in September, an additional 20% in March, and 35% each in June and September next year.
FTSE Russell has estimated the inclusion could redirect up to $6 billion into Vietnam over time. Asset management firm Vanguard said it planned to invest about $2.5 billion over the next year.
Despite optimism about the upgrade, Vietnam's benchmark VN-Index has lost about 0.5% this year, lagging gains of roughly 27% in Thailand and 23% in Singapore, according to LSEG data.
Last year, however, Vietnam was among Southeast Asia's best-performing stock markets as investors positioned themselves for the expected FTSE reclassification.
